nameStory: The Tennessee Warbler got its name from being first described in Tennessee, but this little bird is actually just passing through! Like many warblers, it was named for where scientists first encountered it rather than where it actually lives. The Latin name 'peregrina' means 'wanderer,' which perfectly captures this bird's long-distance migrations.
description: The Tennessee Warbler is a small, active songbird about the size of a chickadee that breeds in northern New England's forests. Males in spring have a clean gray head, white eyebrow stripe, and olive-green back with bright white underparts. Females and fall birds are more yellow-green overall with less contrast. These energetic little birds are constantly on the move, flicking through tree branches as they hunt for insects.

idTips.label: White eyebrow stripe
idTips.description: Look for a bold white line above the eye that contrasts sharply with the gray cap in spring males - it's like a tiny white racing stripe

idTips.label: Clean white underparts
idTips.description: Spring males have bright white bellies and throats with no yellow wash or streaking - they look like they're wearing a crisp white shirt

idTips.label: Thin pointed bill
idTips.description: The bill is noticeably thin and needle-like, perfect for picking tiny insects from leaves - much thinner than a chickadee's seed-cracking bill

idTips.label: Active feeding behavior
idTips.description: Constantly flits and hovers at branch tips, often hanging upside down to reach insects - they never seem to sit still for more than a few seconds

idTips.label: Gray cap
idTips.description: Adult males in breeding plumage have a smooth gray cap that looks like a tiny helmet contrasting with the white eyebrow

habitat: Tennessee Warblers breed in northern New England's coniferous and mixed forests, especially areas with spruce, fir, and birch. During migration, you'll find them in a variety of wooded habitats including parks, gardens, and forest edges. They prefer areas with dense canopy cover where they can hunt for insects among the leaves.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration in May brings males in bright breeding plumage with gray heads and white eyebrows. Listen for their loud, repetitive song that sounds like rapid-fire 'trill-trill-trill' notes.
seasonality.summer: Most continue north to breed, but some nest in northern New England forests. They're busy feeding on spruce budworm caterpillars and other insects.
seasonality.fall: September migration brings duller birds that are more yellow-green overall. Young birds and females can be tricky to identify without the male's distinctive markings.
seasonality.winter: These warblers spend winter in Central and South America, so you won't see them in New England during the cold months.

funFact: Tennessee Warblers are like tiny pest control agents - during spruce budworm outbreaks, their populations can explode by 10 times normal levels as they feast on the caterpillars, with some birds eating over 40 caterpillars per minute!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with the Red-eyed Vireo, which also has a white eyebrow and gray cap. Remember: Tennessee Warblers have thin, pointed bills and are much more active and flittery, while vireos have thicker bills, move more deliberately, and are larger overall.
contextualKnowledge: Like many warblers, the Tennessee Warbler's name is misleading - it doesn't actually live in Tennessee! Most warbler names reflect where ornithologists first collected specimens during migration, not where the birds breed or spend most of their time.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Nashville Warbler, the Tennessee lacks the Nashville's yellow throat and white eye-ring, instead having a clean white throat and white eyebrow stripe. Orange-crowned Warblers are much duller overall with faint orange crown streaks (rarely visible) and lack the Tennessee's bold white eyebrow stripe.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its close relatives, Nashville Warbler is the only one with the gray head and yellow underparts combination.
Orange-crowned Warbler is much duller than its genus relatives - Nashville Warbler has a bold white eyering and gray head, while Tennessee Warbler appears cleaner with whiter underparts.
Among its Leiothlypis relatives, Virginia's Warbler is the only one with the combination of white underparts and yellow undertail coverts.
